name: Gynostemma pentaphyllum (jiaogulan)
lead: Gynostemma pentaphyllum, called jiaogulan or "five-leaf ginseng", is a climbing vine in the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) native to South and East Asia and New Guinea.[1] It is usually drunk as a sweet herbal tea and also sold as extracts and supplements, and is grouped with adaptogen herbs in the longevity category.[1]

Its leaves contain dammarane-type saponins, some identical to ginseng ginsenosides and others called gypenosides, plus polysaccharides, flavonoids and sterols.[1][2][3] Laboratory studies report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, liver-protective and cardiometabolic effects.[2][3][4][5]

Wikipedia states that research is limited, that studies in cardiovascular disease, hyperlipidaemia and type 2 diabetes were too preliminary to conclude benefit, and that no information exists on human toxicity.[1] No study found in these sources tests jiaogulan for appearance outcomes.

paras: According to Wikipedia, the plant was first described in 1406 as a famine food rather than a medicine, and the herbalist Li Shizhen recorded medicinal uses in 1578 while confusing it with a similar herb.[1] The article states it has not been widely used in traditional Chinese medicine and was adopted more broadly only in recent decades.[1]

Reviews catalogue the triterpenoid saponins (gypenosides) as the main bioactive class, alongside polysaccharides and flavonoids.[2][3][6] Rodent studies report anti-inflammatory and liver-protective effects of extracts,[7][8] and a 2018 cell and animal study reported that gypenosides reduced NLRP3 inflammasome activation in a diabetic cardiomyopathy model.[5] Polysaccharide fractions show antioxidant activity in vitro.[9] A review of herbal medicines for cardiovascular disease includes it among the herbs examined.[4]

Registered trials are small and mostly metabolic. They include tea trials in type 2 diabetes (16, 24 and 25 participants),[10][11][12] a 150-person study in metabolic syndrome,[13] an 80-person study of an extract (Actiponin) in obesity,[14] a 100-person weight and fat-loss study of a branded product,[15] a 72-person study on chronic stress-induced strain,[16] and a terminated Phase 2 study of gypenosides in acute optic neuritis (10).[17] The sources consulted give no results for these, and none addresses appearance.

Wikipedia states that toxicity studies exist only in vitro and no information exists on human toxicity.[1] In the European Union it is treated as a novel food following a 2012 court ruling that prohibited its sale as food.[1] A survey of herbal tea products consumed in Thailand measured trace elements in the products and their infusions.[18]

timeline.event: First described, as a famine food.[1]
EU court ruling leads to novel-food status.[1]

card.summary: A sweet adaptogen tea vine with ginseng-like saponins; lab-rich, human data thin, no appearance trials.
card.note: Human toxicity data are lacking; EU treats it as a novel food.

quick.overview:
Jiaogulan is a climbing vine whose leaves are brewed as a sweet tea and sold as an adaptogen and longevity herb. It contains gypenosides, some chemically identical to ginseng saponins.

Research is mostly in cells and animals, with small preliminary human trials on blood sugar and weight. None tests appearance.
quick.mechanism: Gypenosides and polysaccharides are reported to have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory models, including damping of NLRP3 inflammasome signalling.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states there is no information on human toxicity, with toxicity data only in vitro. In the EU it is regulated as a novel food.
